title: Pilot study on the implementation of low-level laser therapy for the prevention of oral mucositis in stem cell transplants.
summary:
Background
Stem cell transplants are used to treat disorders of the haematopoietic and lymphatic systems. Either the patient’s own stem cells or those from another person may be used. Both forms of treatment require very intensive chemotherapy and, in some cases, whole-body radiotherapy. These treatments can cause inflammation and painful damage to the oral mucosa. This inflammation of the oral mucosa is one of the most distressing side effects for patients during treatment. It can lead to longer hospital stays and higher healthcare costs. Pain when swallowing and changes in the sense of taste can also make eating difficult. This can result in weight loss, reduced mobility and a lower quality of life. 
Various steps can be taken to prevent such inflammation. These include patient education, brushing teeth twice daily, mouthwashes, cold treatments and treatment with low-intensity laser light. The effects of laser treatment have not yet been fully researched. However, there is evidence to suggest that it has beneficial effects on cells and tissues. The laser light releases energy in the irradiated cells and can thereby stimulate healing and regeneration processes. For this reason, this treatment is regarded as a promising additional method for the prevention and treatment of inflammation of the oral mucosa following stem cell transplants.
Aim of the study
This pilot study aims to investigate whether the HILARIS FL RED surface laser, manufactured by Heltschl GmbH, is feasible for use in everyday clinical practice. It also seeks to identify the opportunities and challenges associated with introducing the device. The study will examine how user-friendly the device is, how well the treatment is accepted by patients and nursing staff, and how safe it is to use.  The aim of the study is to establish a scientific basis for deciding whether laser treatment should be used in future to prevent inflammation of the oral mucosa in stem cell transplants.
Methodology
The study combines quantitative and qualitative research methods and is being conducted on a stem cell transplant ward at a German university hospital. The study is open to all adult patients who are capable of giving informed consent and who are receiving a stem cell transplant using their own or donor stem cells. Nursing staff who have been trained in the use of the laser device and have used it as part of the study are also participating. 
The user-friendliness, acceptance and safety of the laser device are assessed using questionnaires. Patients complete these after their treatment has finished. The nursing staff complete the questionnaires at the end of the study. In addition, group discussions are held with the nursing staff. In these discussions, experiences, opportunities and potential difficulties associated with the introduction of the device are discussed. The collected data and measurement results are analysed using descriptive statistical methods and presented in tables or diagrams. The findings from the group discussions are analysed using thematic analysis. The MaxQDA software is used for this purpose. Two researchers with experience in qualitative research first analyse the data independently of one another and then jointly.
Finally, the results from both research methods are compared and brought together. This involves examining where the results agree and where there are differences.
